title: The Gravity of the Kuiper Line Anew
premise: Rosalind Montrose has spent thirty years alone on Pluto's moon Charon, tending the Kuiper Line—a greenhouse ark and beacon built for colonists still in cryosleep—and keeping his existence off every registry. When a supply drone delivers a manifest listing a passenger, Ilya Voss, aboard a ship that was never launched, Rosalind realizes someone on Earth knows he's alive and is using the beacon to send a second, hidden transmission loop that will wake only half the sleepers. The choice of which half was encoded decades ago by Rosalind's dead partner, Mara, and the stranger Ilya—Mara's son, born after Rosalind left Earth—arrives to force the beacon's hand. In the end, Rosalind rewrites the loop to wake everyone in slow rotation, sacrificing his own cryo-slot and the garden's power reserve, choosing found family over the loyalty Mara's plan demanded and the truth Ilya came to deliver.
about_author: G. M. Ashgrove is a former botanist for Antarctic research stations who turned to fiction after a decade of tending plants no one would visit for years at a time. Their novels explore loneliness as an act of devotion, and are written in longhand during polar winter.

chapters.title: The Garden at the End of the Manifest
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. He walks his daily circuit through the Kuiper Line greenhouse, narrating his routines to plants that will outlive everyone he knew. The chapter establishes his solitude as devotion, not exile. Emotional beat: quiet contentment with an undercurrent of dread that routine is a form of hiding.

chapters.title: A Ship That Never Flew
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The quarterly supply drone arrives, and its manifest lists the Meridian, a vessel decommissioned before Rosalind was born—with one passenger aboard: Ilya Voss. He checks the beacon logs and finds a transmission fragment he didn't send. Emotional beat: the first crack in thirty years of stillness.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Remembers
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, with flashback. He digs into the beacon's archive and finds Mara's voice buried in the code—a second transmission loop, dormant, addressed to a list of names. He recognizes none of them except the timestamp: the week he left Earth. Emotional beat: betrayal and grief braided together.

chapters.title: Approach Vector
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Aboard the Meridian's shuttle, Ilya reviews his mother's letters and rehearses the speech he's planned for years. He's never met Rosalind; his mother spoke of him only as 'the gardener who ran.' Emotional beat: resentment sharpened by longing for a family he never had.

chapters.title: Docking Protocol for Strangers
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The shuttle docks. Rosalind nearly refuses entry, then sees Ilya's face—Mara's face, younger. He lets him in against every protocol he's kept sacred. Emotional beat: terror of connection outweighed by the hunger for it.

chapters.title: The Half We Keep
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Ilya explains Mara's plan: the hidden loop will wake the genetically and politically vetted half of the sleepers—the 'seed list'—and let the rest drift until resources allow. Rosalind was meant to be the one to fire it. Emotional beat: Ilya's certainty colliding with the gardener's silence.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Tending
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. He shows Ilya the greenhouse—every crop calibrated for a population that may never come—and admits he never opened Mara's final message. Ilya demands he open it now. Rosalind refuses. Emotional beat: loyalty to the dead curdling into avoidance.

chapters.title: Mara's Last Transmission
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Alone, Rosalind finally plays Mara's message: she knew he'd hide, she forgave him, and she named Ilya as the arbiter if Rosalind failed to choose. Ilya, watching the same message from his bunk, learns his mother used him as leverage. Emotional beat: two people gutted by the same dead woman's love.

chapters.title: The Loop Ends in Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Earth's original transmission loop—the one keeping cryosleep systems synced—terminates in ninety days. After that, waking anyone becomes a gamble with their lives. The deadline converts a moral question into a countdown. Emotional beat: dread made mechanical.

chapters.title: Names on the List
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Ilya studies the seed list and finds his own name at the top, and Rosalind's absent. He realizes Mara designed the list to punish the man who left. Emotional beat: the discovery that he was a weapon before he was a son.

chapters.title: The Third Option
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind runs the numbers: the greenhouse's power reserve could wake everyone in staggered rotation—if the garden dies and if someone stays conscious to shepherd the wakes. Someone who can't sleep again. Emotional beat: hope arriving dressed as sacrifice.

chapters.title: Arguments in the Hydroponics Bay
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Ilya calls the third option suicide dressed as virtue; Rosalind calls the seed list murder dressed as mercy. Their fight cracks open old wounds—Mara, abandonment, who owed whom. Emotional beat: anger as the first honest language between them.

chapters.title: What the Plants Know
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A quiet chapter: Rosalind teaches Ilya the garden's rhythms, and in the work they find an uneasy truce. Ilya admits he came less to fire the loop than to meet the man his mother loved more than him. Emotional beat: tenderness emerging from shared labor.

chapters.title: Signal from the Sleeping
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. A cryo-pod telemetry ping reveals one sleeper has been awake for months—Doctor Ansel Reyes, a systems architect who's been silently watching the beacon, waiting to see who would choose. He makes contact. Emotional beat: the story's private world gains a witness, and a threat.

chapters.title: Ansel's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV (first appearance). Reyes has kept his own tally of the sleepers—friends, a daughter—on neither list. He proposes a coup of sorts: seize the beacon, wake the engineers first, decide by committee. Emotional beat: pragmatism that is also grief, and a mirror to both men's certainty.

chapters.title: The Vote of Three
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The three men argue the fate of forty thousand sleepers in a room full of growing things. Ansel's daughter's name forces Rosalind to confront what the seed list would erase; Ilya votes against his own mother's design. Emotional beat: the found family forming exactly at the moment it might fracture.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. Someone begins draining the power reserve—Ansel, it seems, hedging his bets by forcing an early, partial wake. Rosalind races to isolate the breach while the loop clock ticks under thirty days. Emotional beat: trust, newly built, collapsing under pressure.

chapters.title: The Truth About the Meridian
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind discovers the manifest was never a delivery—it was Mara's final test, routed through decades of dead-man switches. Ilya wasn't sent; he was summoned by his mother's ghost in the machine. Emotional beat: the dead woman's hand closing around the living.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Beacon
chapters.summary: Climax, triple POV. At the beacon array, Ansel forces the partial wake; Rosalind physically interposes himself between the override and the loop; Ilya must choose which man to help. He cuts power to the seed list and routes everything into Rosalind's staggered rotation. Emotional beat: love against duty, decided in seconds.

chapters.title: The First to Wake
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV. The first rotation of sleepers opens their eyes to a dying garden and two exhausted keepers. Ansel finds his daughter among them. The cost surfaces: Rosalind's vitals are failing from the shepherd protocol's strain. Emotional beat: victory inseparable from loss.

chapters.title: What the Garden Was For
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Dying, Rosalind walks the greenhouse one last time with Ilya, who now tends it beside him. He finally answers the question he fled Earth to avoid: he stayed invisible because Mara asked him to, and stayed alive because he couldn't stop hoping. Emotional beat: peace earned, not granted.

chapters.title: The Kuiper Line, Anew
chapters.summary: Ilya's POV, epilogue. A year later, the colony's first harvest comes in; the beacon now broadcasts outward, inviting rather than concealing. Ilya plants a row in his mother's name and another in Rosalind's, and writes the manifest for the next supply run himself. Emotional beat: grief transformed into continuation; the family, found, holds.
